@@126351715 <h> Canadian dispatches from Israel at wartime : Like father , like daughter <p> One of the defining memories of my youth is the 1990 Gulf War , and the subsequent Iraqi missile attacks against Israel early the next year . I was 14 , and I distinctly remember the drama of waking up at night to the sounds of air raid sirens warning of incoming Scud missiles . In a haze , I would rush to our bomb shelter , put on my gas mask and wonder if Saddam Hussein had deployed his chemical weapons against us . <p> The attacks generated plenty of fear and disruption -- but no chemicals and very few casualties -- and in just over a month it was over , remaining etched in my mind as a singular teenage experience . <p> I still reflect upon that time as an exciting , rather than anxious , episode that sparked my interest in geopolitics and likely influenced my eventual career choice of journalism . From the confines of our shelter , I would listen to the breaking news on a transistor radio and try @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ returning to school , I penned a spirited first-person essay for my English class about the ordeal that became my first foray into news writing . <p> Little could I have imagined that 35 years later , my oldest daughter would be experiencing her own defining missile attack experience at roughly the same age . Now that the rumbling jets overhead have fallen silent and a ceasefire seems to have taken hold ( at least for now ) , it is my fervent hope that one day she will be able to look back at the 12 days of attacks from Iran with the same , albeit somewhat twisted , sense of nostalgia that I do about those that arrived from Iraq . Perhaps this too will merely remain a colourful memory of her youth ? <p> Honestly , I 'm skeptical . The Iran of today is not the Iraq of yesteryear , and she is simply growing up in a far more dangerous world . <p> The war adventure of my youth was an aberration from an otherwise mostly insulated childhood in Israel . In my formative years @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Israeli and Palestinian front , and Iran and Iraq were busy fighting each other . This prompted my first lesson in Mideast politics when , inspired by sports and Star Wars , I naively asked my father who we were rooting for in that latter showdown . He dryly responded : both . <p> He was right . Once their eight-year war was over , Iran and Iraq each finally had the bandwidth to focus their ire on a greater adversary : us . Looking to break a U.S.-backed coalition , Iraq began firing missiles at Israel in the first Gulf War and then threatened to do so again in the second Gulf War a decade later . All the while , Iran was busy building a nuclear program and establishing a ring of extremist militant proxies that posed a far greater threat to Israel . ( That inspired a second memorable regional insight from my father . Following George W. Bush 's hasty post-9/11 assault on Iraq , he suggested that if the Americans were already hellbent on bombing radical Mideast nations that started with the letters IRA @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Still , all of this had very little impact on my daily life growing up in Israel . For my daughter , though , it has been entirely different . I first had to shuffle her to safety as an infant during rocket attacks from Gaza in the 2014 war , so this risk has been ever-present for nearly her entire life . Back in 1991 , Israel was a sideshow , and the missiles were a diversion . However , in the past decade , we have become the main event , as the primary targets of projectiles from Gaza , Lebanon , Yemen , Iraq and Iran . <p> Objectively , we are far more protected . Since the 1990s , reinforced safe rooms have been required in all new housing and the country has expanded its network of bomb shelters and invested heavily in early warning systems and public readiness . Israel has also developed a multilayer missile defense system that provides unprecedented interception capabilities . <p> But from a cognitive ( and a child 's ) perspective , Israel has been constantly under threat for a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . As her political awareness has expanded with age , she often expresses a sentiment that it seems as if the whole world is against us . <p> For my daughter 's generation , a reality of sirens , missile attacks and disruption has been normalized . Since Oct. 7 , 2023 , it has almost become a way of life . <p> A child from her school was abducted to Gaza on that horrible day and she has since experienced frequent mad dashes to nearby shelters to escape rocket attacks . Once , while waiting for a bus home after school , she did n't even have time for that and had no choice but to lie face down on the hot pavement as sirens wailed . She then heard a loud explosion and picked up her head to see smoke billowing from an impact in the distance . <p> In retrospect , my teenage wartime experience was exciting because it was unusual , and it also had a clear beginning and end . For my daughter , though , it 's been more of the same -- only @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ this latest war , and optimism of a broader long-lasting shift in the Mideast , there is still so much uncertainty about what lies ahead . It 's enough to make any parent truly worry about what kind of future awaits his or her children . <p> Being a parent inherently involves the ageless and global plight of concern for one 's offspring . But in Israel , it is far more visceral and present . Mandatory military service is always on the horizon and there are just too many people in your immediate and extended circles who have been harmed . <p> Lord knows , my parents worried a lot about me , too : as a soldier in the army , as a civilian amid bus bombings , as a journalist covering war and terror . But their worry never seemed to translate into an existential angst for the long-term wellbeing of the country or shatter their faith of continuing to live in it . <p> My parents chose to make Israel their home and they told my siblings and I that as American , Canadian and Israeli @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on the matter when we came of age . Despite my many deliberations , I also eventually lay down roots here , just as my siblings have . <p> So , it was with a heavy heart that during a recent rude middle of the night awakening to sirens , I heard my 13-year-old daughter offhandedly remark that if she were ever to have children , she would raise them elsewhere . <p> That stopped me in my tracks , taking me back to my own adolescent ambivalence . All I could do at that moment was repeat my own parents ' words and tell her that when she is older , she too will be able to make that choice on her own . I just hope that by then , Israel will have recovered from its nadir of recent years , and there will still be a legitimate choice to be made . <h> Author <h> Support Our Mission : Make a Difference ! <p> The Canadian Jewish News is now a Registered Journalism Organization ( RJO ) as defined by the Canada Revenue Agency . @@126392595 <h> Jewish students grapple with convocations becoming political battlegrounds <p> Syd Palter tied an Israeli flag to her wrist at her convocation at the University of Toronto , June , 2024 . ( Photo supplied ) . <p> When valedictorian Salahuddin Said approached the podium , the customary applause rippled warmly in the convocation hall at University of Waterloo . <p> Draped prominently around his neck was a keffiyeh , the checkered pattern stark and purposeful against his academic regalia . <p> A Bachelor of Applied Science graduate in mechanical engineering , Said delivered a speech that was mostly typical during this June ceremony . He cracked inside jokes about course material , about connections forged among students , and spoke about the ethical responsibilities of engineers . Eventually , however , he departed from his pre-approved speech . <p> " I must direct your attention to the ethical catastrophe in Israel 's genocide in Gaza , where technology developed by engineers has been used by Israel to target and bomb civilians , over 60,000 of which have been killed , including aid workers , journalists , and entire family @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ every university like the one we stand in today , " he said . <p> " As an engineer , I am obligated to join the 6,000 other students in again calling upon the University of Waterloo to sever ties with Israel 's Technion Institute for its role in developing weapons used against civilians and infrastructure in Gaza . " <p> Nick Manning , associate vice-president of communications at the University of Waterloo , said in an email to The CJN that Said 's delivered speech was not the draft approved by the convocation committee . " At Waterloo , freedom of expression is foundational , " Manning wrote . " We review valedictorian speeches in advance . The remarks shared were modified from what had been submitted . " <p> One mother of a Jewish graduating student , who did not wish to use her name , expressed disappointment . " This was not a political event , and it 's not the place for this . He 's supposed to represent all of the students . And he did n't . " <p> Jay Solomon , chief advancement @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " A student used what should be a joyous moment to take a position singling out Jewish students , calling on the university to sever ties with an academic institution in the world 's only Jewish state , " he told The CJN , mentioning that similar incidents have occurred at Ontario graduation ceremonies over the last two years . <p> In a social media post , Hillel Ontario urged the University of Waterloo to condemn the speech and reaffirm its partnership with Technion , calling the speech " divisive and discriminatory . " <p> " By implying that the university , and by extension its graduates , are complicit in ' genocide , ' he not only shamed his fellow graduates and their families but also alienated the Jewish community and all those who support Israel or who have benefited from studying at the Technion . It was a discriminatory and deeply inappropriate accusation that had no place at a graduation ceremony . " <p> This case , however , was not an anomaly . <p> Across Canadian universities , convocations -- meant to celebrate academic achievement -- have @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ told The CJN they would skip graduation ceremonies this year , feeling unsupported by administrations . Others chose to demonstrate solidarity with Israel openly , wearing hostage pins , symbols , and Israeli flags . At least one Jewish student at an Ontario university was physically assaulted for making such a choice , The CJN has learned . <p> Yet , even for those who wish to celebrate academic milestones without political controversy , neutrality is becoming increasingly elusive . <p> Institutional neutrality versus student expression <p> The University of Waterloo recently shared a statement about freedom of expression and institutional neutrality , posted on its website . The statement includes recommendations detailed from the school 's Task Force on Freedom of Expression and Inclusive Engagement . <p> According to that statement , members of the university community often urge institutional leaders to publicly respond to social , political or moral issues , but taking an institutional stance can stifle the diverse views essential to campus debate . Instead , the statement said , Waterloo sees its role as providing support for individual expression , recognizing these issues as central @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to address publicly . <p> " Adopting a position of institutional neutrality and institutional restraint allows us to safeguard our mission and ensure that the University remains a place where individuals can engage freely and robustly with ideas from all perspectives , without the chilling effect that may result from institutional endorsement of a particular view , " the statement reads . <p> Manning clarified the university 's stance , given recent criticism towards the convocation committee 's inaction toward Said 's comments . " I want to be clear with you that the views expressed are those of the individual and self-evidently , given the criticism levelled at the university , are not the views of the institution , " he wrote . <p> He added that the comments made did not warrant any action to be taken during the speech . <p> Jacqueline Dressler , director of advocacy for Hillel Ontario , pointed out that Said 's speech has been posted publicly by the university without any condemnation . <p> " By sharing the unedited video of the ceremony on the Faculty of Engineering website , the university @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the speech , " Dressler said , in an email statement to The CJN . <p> " Not only was the speaker able to continue with the unapproved remarks , with no condemnation , but the school is continuing to promote it . " <p> Students skipping convocations <p> Other students , who chose to remain anonymous , said they have opted out of attending their convocation ceremonies this June , frustrated by administrations ' failures to address antisemitism on campus . <p> " I do n't trust my school 's administration to leave anti-Israel stuff out of the ceremony , " one student said , with an upcoming convocation at Toronto Metropolitan University ( TMU ) . <p> Other students feel isolated from their cohort , feeling that their student colleagues have demonized their Jewish identity . " After seeing so much of their anti-Israel stuff posted on Instagram , I could n't just sit next to them in my gown and pretend everything is normal , " said another student , who skipped a graduation at York University in June . <p> High school ceremonies caught in controversy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ valedictorian at a west Ottawa high school made remarks about Gaza this convocation season , which prompted the school to tell her not to attend her classes on Monday . <p> " I must acknowledge colonial and genocidal atrocities today , including the massacre of more than 17,000 Palestinian children in Gaza , " said Elizabeth Yao , during her commencement speech for Bell High School . <p> As reported by CBC , an email by the school 's principal , sent to parents after the ceremony , said that Yao " intentionally took focus away from the purpose of the event , celebrating the achievement of our graduating class . " <p> While valedictorians declaring political messages beyond the confines of pre-approved scripts has become more normal in recent years , a much more common form of protest has been wearing symbolic garments . <p> A Jewish teacher from a private Toronto high school described a recent graduation that saw numerous students wearing keffiyehs . <p> One of these students " blatantly folded her arms and looked right at me , as if to say , ' What are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ teacher recalled . The families chose to leave , sparking further controversy . " The school is now receiving backlash for appearing pro-Israel , " the teacher explained . " But they really only acted swiftly to keep the ceremony apolitical . " <p> " The faculty at TMU has failed their Jewish students time and time again , " wrote SSI in the post 's caption . " <p> The CJN emailed TMU 's convocation committee to learn more about dress code restrictions for graduation ceremonies and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ceremonies , but did not receive a reply . <p> ' Do n't let them take this away ' <p> Last June , Syd Palter sat quietly in the convocation hall at the University of Toronto , her fingers tracing the small Israeli flag she 'd knotted around her wrist . Around her , the auditorium buzzed gently with anticipation as hundreds of students gathered to celebrate the academic milestone . <p> The previous fall , in 2023 , Palter had been in Israel on Oct. 7 , beginning a semester abroad when conflict erupted , reshaping her life irrevocably . To graduate on time , she 'd completed a rigorous 70-page essay -- a capstone requirement for her joint JD/MBA program -- which she chose to focus on the Israel-Palestine conflict from a legal perspective . @@126492397 <p> When I saw that my Bluesky feed was smitten with a New York City mayoral candidate , a state assemblyman named Zohran Mamdani , I thought a few things . First , I figured , if Bluesky is 100% behind a candidate , this person stands no chance . I was seeing things about free buses and rent freezes and thinking , yes , it tracks that progressive-heavy platform Bluesky wants this . Remember the old saying , Twitter is n't real life ? Bluesky is even less representative of anything . Then again , I thought Hillary would win . Do n't go to me for prognostication . <p> Next , I thought , wait a second , I do n't live in New York City ! What did I care who became its mayor , let alone in who won a Democratic mayoral primary ? It felt a bit like having to care about the goings-on of Harvard University . OK , not quite , because I 'm from NYC , and more to the point , because this is an objectively high-stakes election involving a city @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , economic , and political impact . The importance here is more than symbolic . This was still not enough to get me to sit down and read the candidates ' platforms and pick which one I would vote for if I could vote in that election , which I can not . <p> Third , I immediately registered the fact that Mamdani is good-looking . Our society is weird about male beauty , pretending not to see it . Women in particular may be reluctant to speak about it because we get accused of being too frivolous for politics . But I am not afraid to say it : Mamdani is a conventionally attractive man , in the visual tradition of Barack Obama and Justin Trudeau . Do I think his floppy-haired heartthrob looks singlehandedly explain his popularity ? No -- policies , charisma , and timing all play a role . But yeah it mattered that he 's cute . <p> It took me longer than it should have to give any thought any which way about what Mamdani 's candidacy means for Jews , or indeed that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ first Muslim mayor . ( He is of Indian-American heritage and was born in Uganda . ) This is either the most or least significant thing about this story , depending whom you ask . <p> *** <p> I witnessed much rejoicing on Bluesky over what it means that New York , such a Jewish city , went for Mamdani , some going so far as to claim that this is itself evidence of the spuriousness of the antisemitism claims against him . Numerically , though , a candidate succeeding in New York is neither here nor there . It 's Jewish as cities go , but approximately seven out of eight New Yorkers are not Jewish . A Democrat 's success in New York could indicate Jewish support , but would n't necessarily . <p> If a candidate 's votes came almost exclusively from that non-Jewish majority , then that candidate could be neither here nor there where Jews are concerned , or even catering to disparate groups who 've found common cause in hating Jews . New York Times columnist Michelle Goldberg gives as additional evidence for the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Jews Love Zohran Mamdani , " that " he won most of Park Slope , a neighborhood full of progressive Jews , and held his own on the similarly Jewish Upper West Side . " Again , this could point to Jewish support , but it could also mean that the non-Jews in these areas are not so keen on their Jewish neighbours . Such things have , historically , happened . <p> It is not yet known how Jews voted in this election . There was ranked-choice voting , something I am not enough of a shape rotator to fully understand , but that means that you could put some support to a candidate without them being your top pick . This was also , remember , a Democratic primary . Republican Jews , often but not always Orthodox , were n't voting in it . Assuming the handful of antizionist left-wing ( mostly-young ) Jews voted for Mamdani and that the handful of MAGA-supporting Jews who are for some reason registered Democrats went for former New York governor Andrew Cuomo , where did this leave the rest ? @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ some clues on closer to a block-by-block basis . The purple areas are the ones that went to Lander , suggesting that bits of the Upper West Side and the really bookish parts of Brooklyn were on board for progressivism minus the anti-Israel bit ( or , that Lander is for some unrelated reason known and popular in those areas ) . Some reporting conveys that American Jews are having a range of different feelings , which is both true and tricky in terms of gauging how many feel which way . <p> There 's a difference between treating a candidate 's stance on Israel as a litmus test and giving it any consideration whatsoever . And in this election , rather a lot was going on beyond ' so do we pick the Free Palestine guy or not ? ' Cuomo -- who was n't even the Jewish candidate -- had positioned himself as the pro-Jewish pick , maybe earnestly or maybe to distract from sexual misconduct allegations against him . Cuomo , with wealthy donors and former president Bill Clinton 's seal of approval , represented the establishment @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> A lot of Jews -- Jewish Democrats especially -- are also women , for whom #MeToo considerations may loom larger than geopolitical ones . ( Not that women ca n't care about international affairs , not that men ca n't object to sexual harassment , do n't come at me ! ) A lot , too , are young people , or people of all ages concerned about the cost of living , who may be drawn to Mamdani 's democratic socialism . The way progressive causes now get bundled into an omnicause , it 's possible that many do share Mamdani 's Mideast politics , but it 's not at all hard for me to picture a voter who cares very much about Israel 's continued existence putting other things first in what is , after all , a local election in America . <p> I can also see being a Jewish voter and witnessing a US Congressman calling for Mamdani to be deported , as Andy Ogles of Tennessee did on X , and wanting no part in this , even tangentially . This , even though @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that candidate . <p> Mostly , though , I can see feeling energized by Mamdani 's win as a sign of pushback against Trump . I do feel this , albeit with the obvious reservations . For what it 's worth , I think he 's onto something regarding free buses . <p> What we 're looking at is something more complicated than David Frum 's suggestion that antisemitism now thriving in New York . Just as ' antisemitic but pro-Israel ' is a spot on the political spectrum , so too , evidently , is ' anti-Israel but friend of Jews and not just the three who are antizionists . ' So everything 's dandy , right ? <p> *** <p> The question of whether Mamdani is or is not , personally , an antisemite is not a productive conversation . It is a blood-pressure-raising shouting match between people who jump to the term too readily , sometimes for bigoted reasons ( ' Muslim and born in Uganda ' is awfully close to the xenophobic smears against Barack Obama , except in Mamdani 's case , this is his @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on ) , and ones who effectively would n't characterize any left-wing antisemitism as such . <p> This much is clear : Mamdani has long has been a pro-Palestinian activist . That is not my assumption based on his heritage but a fact about the views he openly espouses . He is also opposed to antisemitism , and prepared to make common cause with Jewish progressives whose views about Israel are not his own . To my knowledge he did not say , globalize the intifada , rather he refused to denounce the expression . His ( as I interpret it ) one-state-solution ideal for Israel would have the result of ending Israel as a Jewish state , which is ... yeah , not my position , nor that of all but a handful of Jews . His antizionism goes beyond criticism of Israel 's actions in Gaza and the West Bank -- criticisms that I see as if anything necessary from a pro-Israel perspective . <p> We can get into abstract philosophical discussions about whether that sort of antizionism amounts to antisemitism ( and I 'm going to be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but also that Mamdani is not , personally , an antisemite ) , and still be nowhere closer to figuring out what sort of mayor Mamdani would be for New York 's Jews . <p> What 's hard to assess from afar , even reading up on it , is how much Mamdani is presenting himself as a breath of fresh air for pro-Palestine voters , and how much this is a marginal topic for him that gets dragged up by his detractors . It could be that this was like during the 2024 US presidential elections , where the Democrats were successfully taken to task for a level of ' woke ' that far exceeded their actual platform . <p> *** <p> The takeaway from this election result is less about antisemitism or geopolitics and more about New York 's receding distinctly Jewish character . Asians are the new Jews , halal is the new kosher , things of that nature . I point this out not to make some kind of sinister point about replacement but to remind that cities evolve . New York still has a ton @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is noteworthy when you consider our relative numbers globally , or for that matter in Toronto . But the New York Jews of 2025 are not the New York Jews of 1995 or 1955 . Assimilation and its opposite have both contributed to these shifts , as have factors outside the Jewish community . <p> When I , someone who depending how you count these things last lived fully in New York City in 2009 , find myself thinking Toronto seems less Jewy than my hometown , I 'm not entirely wrong , but I 'm also comparing a place that currently exists with one that did 20 years ago . <p> Delis , Seinfeld , whatever your reference point , we 're not in that world . Whether its closest cultural heir is the Jewish Currents-reading , Mamdani-voting Bushwick-residing 25-year-old or the single-and-mingling Modern Orthodox West 96th Streeter , or a Hamptons-going super-posh sort whose only difference from her WASP equivalents is that she cares a smidge more about Israel , or an Israeli expat or a Bukharan immigrant or a Borough Park Hasid or someone else entirely , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ not say . All I know is that Mario Cuomo , father of Andrew and source of his name recognition , was himself governor of New York between the years 1983 and 1994 , aka the first eleven years of my life . If Andrew Cuomo was the nostalgia candidate , maybe nostalgia was n't enough . <h> Author <p> Phoebe is the opinion editor for The Canadian Jewish News and a contributor editor of The CJN 's Scribe Quarterly print magazine .
